text: This Friday is a Friday the 13th, a day steeped in superstition.
label: content

text: So in its honor, we're talking a bit about the language of superstition.
label: content

text: Consider these three phrases.
label: content

text: I've never gotten a speeding ticket.
label: content

text: She was Ophelia in Macbeth.
label: content

text: It's awfully quiet tonight.
label: content

text: What did these very different sentences have in common?
label: content

text: Well, the first might evoke a warning from your passengers not to press your luck.
label: content

text: The second will tell all your theater nerd friends that you're well, not a theater nerd.
label: content

text: And the third might get you shooed out of the hospital cafeteria.
label: content

text: All three phrases involve superstitions.
label: content

text: And often those superstitions show up in language that makes it seem like we believe what we
label: content

text: say or don't say will somehow affect the outcome of a situation.
label: content

text: So let's start with the speeding ticket scenario.
label: content

text: You may have a spotless driving record, but if you brag about that out loud, well, you're
label: content

text: tempting fate.
label: content

text: Your passengers might say, don't jinx it.
label: content

text: This is if the speakers believe that never mentioning your history with speeding tickets
label: content

text: will somehow magically prevent you from ever getting one.
label: content

text: And magical is a pretty appropriate term here because the word jinx may come from a word
label: content

text: associated with magic.
label: content

text: Merriam-Webster dates the noun form of jinx, spelled J-I-N-X, to 1902 and the verb to 1913.
label: content

text: It says the word might be an alteration of J-Y-N-X.
label: content

text: spelling comes from Jinx Torquia, the scientific name of the Rhineck, a small woodpecker.
label: content

text: When a predator approaches a Rhineck's nesting hole, it twists its neck and writhes in an
label: content

text: alarming way, hissing like a snake.
label: content

text: Rural Europeans who saw that unsettling display came to connect the birds with dark omens,
label: content

text: curses, and witchcraft.
label: content

text: But it's important to point out that Merriam-Webster treats the origins of Jinx as a maybe, not
label: content

text: an absolute etymological origin story. Still, we do know that early 20th century baseball
label: content

text: helped spread the modern use of jinks. A 1910 newspaper explained that players called a person
label: content

text: or thing bringing bad luck a jinks, and pitcher Christie Matheson mentioned a baseball jinks
label: content

text: in his 1912 book Pitching in a Pinch. So in baseball, speakers fear talking about success
label: content

text: while it's happening. But in the theatre? Well, even saying the name of a certain play
label: content

text: can supposedly be dangerous. Let's say you're entering a theatre to watch your friend perform
label: content

text: in a play. As you take a program, you tell the usher your friend played Ophelia in Macbeth.
label: content

text: And then, the eyes of all the theatre-goers around you widen in horror or narrow with disdain.
label: content

text: Why? Because you have committed a major theatre faux pas. You don't say Macbeth inside a theatre.
label: content

text: She played a filia? Would have been enough. No need to mention the play.
label: content

text: Or if you really wanted to have fun with it, you could have said the Scottish play, or even Mackers or Macbethsy.
label: content

text: Just not Macbeth. Because if you say that taboo word, you might be evicted from the theatre until you complete a little ritual
label: content

text: ritual like spinning three times, spitting, cursing, and then knocking to be let back
label: content

text: in.
label: transition

text: Or you might have to recite a line from a Shakespeare play with less death and violence
label: content

text: like say, a Midsummer Night's Dream.
label: content

text: Lord, what fools these mortals be!
label: content

text: The word taboo first showed up in English in 1777 and, according to the Oxford English
label: content

text: Dictionary, referred to things that were quote, prohibited to the general population because
label: content

text: they were regarded as sacred, supernatural, or restricted to the use of a chief or priest."
label: content

text: That first use was in James Cook's book, A Voyage to the Pacific Ocean, and the OED
label: content

text: says it referred to, quote, the cultural or religious customs of various islands of the
label: content

text: Pacific, unquote.
label: content

text: But the origin is still a little unclear.
label: content

text: It may have come from a Tongan word tapu or a Maori word with the same spelling in New
label: content

text: New Zealand. But they say it was probably reinforced by cognates in other oceanic languages too,
label: content

text: such as Samoan, Tahitian, Fijian, and so on.
label: content

text: Getting back to Shakespeare, there's a legend about this curse being ancient, but it might
label: content

text: be a lot more modern than it seems. The standard story goes that Shakespeare incorporated real
label: content

text: witchcraft into the play, and that offended real witches who supposedly cursed it. There's
label: content

text: Also a story about Lady Macbeth's actor dying and being replaced, but there's no real supporting evidence.
label: content

text: Even so, once the play had earned a reputation for being cursed, anything that happened during
label: content

text: a production of Macbeth became a kind of evidence, including the infamous disaster in 1849,
label: content

text: the Aster Place riot.
label: content

text: It was sparked by a rivalry between two famous actors, an aristocratic British star and a
label: content

text: rugged American favorite, who were both playing Macbeth at the same time in New York City.
label: content

text: Things boiled over when a working-class mob of more than 10,000 people stormed with the
label: content

text: British actor's upscale theater, turning a petty theatrical feud into a deadly riot.
label: content

text: Paul Menzer, a Shakespearean scholar, searched for information about the curse while researching
label: content

text: his book, Anecdotal Shakespeare.
label: content

text: He reported that he couldn't find any mention of the curse until around the 1930s.
label: content

text: He also found that in the 18th century, the unlucky Shakespeare play was supposedly a
label: content

text: different play, all's well that ends well.
label: content

text: The Royal Shakespeare Company gives us another plausible idea.
label: content

text: A struggling company might stage Macbeth as a sort of financial rescue.
label: content

text: So when Macbeth shows up on a theatre's schedule, it could be a sign that the theatre is already
label: content

text: in trouble. So the theater itself seems ripe for rumors and superstition. But the last place
label: content

text: you probably expect taboo words to show up is among professionals whose whole careers
label: content

text: center around scientific evidence. In hospitals, especially in emergency and on-call settings,
label: content

text: you simply do not say it's quiet. In fact, you avoid the Q word altogether. There's
label: content

text: There's no real known origin for this word-related superstition, but medical literature documents
label: content

text: it across countries and specialties.
label: content

text: It even shows up in veterinary emergency medicine.
label: content

text: And yep, researchers have tested the Q word to see if there's anything to the longstanding
label: content

text: practice of avoiding it.
label: content

text: One 2019 study looked at 61 days in a hospital microbiology department.
label: content

text: In some days, chosen randomly, someone would say, today will be a quiet day.
label: content

text: On other days, they avoided the word altogether and, shocker, the researchers found no significant
label: content

text: difference in workloads on the days where people avoided the word quiet.
label: content

text: A narrative review featured in the Emergency Medicine Journal attempted to synthesize data
label: content

text: across other studies on the word quiet to see whether it had an effect on clinical workload.
label: content

text: But none of that research showed that using or avoiding the word made any meaningful difference,
label: content

text: other than sometimes changing people's perception of how demanding their workloads became if
label: content

text: the Q word showed up.
label: content

text: But humans have probably always been superstitious.
label: content

text: The word itself is quite old too.
label: content

text: Superstition goes back to the early 1300s, but it has always carried a sense of a belief
label: content

text: that is excessive, false, or irrational.
label: content

text: It came to English partly from Latin and partly from French.
label: content

text: And the OED says that in middle French,
label: content

text: it especially referred to things
label: content

text: that were non-Christian or heretical.
label: content

text: The Latin it comes from means to stand,
label: content

text: but Edamon Lyon says nobody is sure
label: content

text: how it got from that meaning
label: content

text: to the fear of the supernatural meaning.
label: content

text: One possibility is that it comes from people standing stiff
label: content

text: or stunned in awe,
label: content

text: but that's just one of many possibilities.
label: content

text: Ultimately, superstitious phrases
label: content

text: us navigate uncertainty, but they don't seem to affect reality. They show up when we're trying
label: content

text: to control outcomes we don't have full control over like our health and safety, winning streaks,
label: content

text: live performances, and even emergency medicine. Some experiments have even found that performing
label: content

text: a ritual can reduce anxiety and sometimes even improve performance. But that's not because
label: content

text: the ritual is changing fate so much as affecting the mental state of the person who performs it.
